specPoints.text: know the definitions of amplitude, wavefront, frequency, wavelength and period of a wave

primer.text: Waves only make sense once you can measure them. This lesson fixes the five measuring words of wave motion in place: the wavefront you draw from above, the amplitude of a swing, the wavelength between matching points, the frequency of passes per second and the period of a single pass. Every later wave calculation leans on these.

lessons.title: Wavefronts
lessons.opening: Seen from above, a moving wave can be drawn as a set of parallel lines, each standing for one wave: the wavefronts. Their spacing does real work in diagrams, because crowded lines mean a short wavelength and widely spaced lines mean a long one. The arrow showing travel direction is called a ray.
keyPoints: Each wavefront line represents a single wave drawn as if viewed from above.
The arrow showing the direction a wave moves is called a ray.
The gap between neighbouring wavefronts represents the wavelength.
Close-spaced wavefronts show a short wavelength; far-spaced ones show a long wavelength.

low.restatement: Wavefronts are the top-down picture of a wave: one line per wave, with the spacing between the lines standing in for the wavelength.
low.analogy: Aerial photo of ocean swells: each bright crest line is a wavefront, and bunched lines mean choppy short waves.
low.examPointer: Diagram questions often want the ray arrow as well as the wavefront lines, so always add the direction arrow.

medium.restatement: The wavefront picture trades the up-down profile for a map view: what you lose in shape detail you gain in being able to show refraction and direction changes cleanly.
medium.analogy: A contour map replaces a mountain photograph with lines whose spacing tells you the steepness at a glance.
medium.examPointer: When wavefronts bend at a boundary, the spacing change tells you the speed change; quote that link in refraction questions.

check.stem: A wavefront is best described as:

options.text: the highest point of a wave
options.explanation: That is the peak, a profile feature rather than a map-view line.

options.text: a line representing one wave, drawn as if viewed from above
options.explanation: Wavefront lines are the top-down representation of successive waves.
That is the time period.

options.text: the number of waves per second
options.explanation: That is the frequency.

check.stem: On a wavefront diagram, the arrow showing where the wave is heading is called:

options.explanation: The normal is the construction line at right angles to a boundary.
A crest is a profile peak, not an arrow.
The direction arrow of a wave is called a ray.
Troughs are profile features, not direction markers.

check.stem: Wavefront lines drawn close together indicate:

options.explanation: Long wavelengths give widely spaced lines.
Spacing shows wavelength, not the size of the swing.
Spacing is a spatial measure, not a time measure.
Bunched wavefronts mean the matching points of successive waves are near each other.

check.stem: Two wavefront diagrams show the same kind of wave. In the first, the lines are twice as far apart as in the second. The first wave has:

options.explanation: Wider spacing between matching points means a proportionally longer wavelength.
That would follow from narrower spacing, not wider.
The spacing is what encodes the wavelength.
Amplitude is a separate measurement from spacing.

check.stem: Which statement about wavefront diagrams is true?

options.text: each line stands for one full oscillation in time
options.explanation: The diagram maps space, not time.

options.text: the lines show the medium moving upwards
options.explanation: Wavefronts map the wave, not a vertical motion of the material.

options.text: each line stands for a whole single wave
options.explanation: One wavefront represents one wave in the top-down picture.

options.text: the lines must always be evenly curved
options.explanation: Wavefronts can be straight or curved depending on the source.

check.stem: State what the space between two neighbouring wavefronts represents.
check.modelAnswer: It represents the wavelength, the distance between matching points of successive waves.

check.stem: Name the line drawn at right angles to a boundary that angles are measured from in reflection diagrams.
check.modelAnswer: That construction line is called the normal.

check.stem: Explain why crowded wavefront lines are read as a short wavelength.
check.modelAnswer: Each line marks the same point of the next wave, so when the lines sit close together the distance between matching points of successive waves is small, and that distance is the wavelength.

check.stem: A pond sketch shows straight parallel wavefront lines with an arrow pointing north. State what the arrow and the line spacing each tell you.
check.modelAnswer: The arrow (the ray) gives the direction of travel, northwards, and the spacing between the wavefront lines gives the wavelength of the ripples.

lessons.title: Amplitude & wavelength
sourceHeadings: Using a graph to determine wavelength and amplitude
lessons.opening: Two lengths describe the shape of a wave on paper. Amplitude measures the size of the swing: the rise from the undisturbed level to a peak, or the drop to a trough. Wavelength measures the repeat distance: from any chosen point on the wave to the matching point on the next wave.
keyPoints: Amplitude is the distance from the undisturbed position to a peak or a trough.
Amplitude carries the symbol A and is measured in metres.
Wavelength is the distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave.
Wavelength carries the symbol lambda and is measured in metres.
On a displacement-distance graph, wavelength is read between matching points along the horizontal axis.

low.restatement: Amplitude says how far the wave swings from its resting level, and wavelength says how far along the wave you must go before the shape repeats.
low.analogy: A fairground swing: amplitude is how high it flies, wavelength is how many metres between one swing and the next rider at the same height.
low.examPointer: Read amplitude from the rest line, never from trough to peak; the rest line is the reference examiners mark against.

medium.restatement: Amplitude tracks the energy carried by the oscillation while wavelength tracks the spatial repeat unit; the two are independent measurements you read from different directions on a graph.
medium.analogy: On a mountain trail profile, amplitude is the height of each hump above the valley floor and wavelength is the distance from one summit to the next.
medium.examPointer: Wavelength can be measured between any corresponding points, not only peak-to-peak; state that when a diagram lacks clear peaks.

check.stem: Amplitude is measured from:

options.explanation: Peak-to-trough spans double the amplitude.

options.text: the undisturbed position to a peak or trough
options.explanation: Amplitude is the swing size relative to the resting level.

options.text: one peak to the next peak
options.explanation: That distance is the wavelength.
That describes travel distance, not wave anatomy.

check.stem: The symbol and unit of wavelength are:

options.explanation: A is the symbol for amplitude.
f is frequency, measured in hertz.
T is the time period.
Wavelength uses the Greek letter lambda and is measured in metres.

check.stem: On a displacement-distance graph, the wavelength is read:

options.text: along the horizontal axis between matching points
options.explanation: Wavelength is a distance, so it is read horizontally between corresponding points.

options.text: vertically from the rest line to a peak
options.explanation: That vertical reading gives the amplitude.

options.text: along the horizontal axis between a peak and the next trough
options.explanation: That span is half a wavelength.

options.text: it cannot be read from a graph
options.explanation: Graphs are precisely where these values are read in exams.

check.stem: A wave on a graph rises 4 cm above the rest line and dips 4 cm below it. The amplitude is:

options.explanation: That is the peak-to-trough span, twice the amplitude.
No halving is involved; the swing is 4 cm each way.
Amplitude runs from the undisturbed level to one extreme, so 4 cm.
Nothing in the graph multiplies the reading fourfold.

check.stem: A longer wavelength on the same style of graph appears as:

options.explanation: Peak height sets amplitude, not wavelength.
Longer wavelength means the pattern repeats over a greater distance.
The rest line is a reference, unchanged by wavelength.

options.text: more repeats in the same horizontal span
options.explanation: That is a shorter wavelength.

check.stem: State the definition of amplitude.
check.modelAnswer: Amplitude is the height from the undisturbed resting level out to a peak or to a trough of a wave.

check.stem: State the definition of wavelength.
check.modelAnswer: Wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next crest, or from one trough to the next trough.

check.stem: Explain why peak-to-trough height is not the amplitude.
check.modelAnswer: Amplitude is defined from the undisturbed rest level to one extreme, and the peak-to-trough span crosses from one extreme to the other, covering that distance twice.

check.stem: A displacement-distance graph shows successive peaks 0.5 m apart on the horizontal axis. State the wavelength, and give the amplitude if the peaks stand 3 cm above the rest line.
check.modelAnswer: The wavelength is 0.5 m, read between matching points horizontally, and the amplitude is 3 cm, read vertically from the undisturbed level to a peak.

lessons.title: Frequency & time period
sourceHeadings: Using a graph to determine time period
lessons.opening: The last pair of measuring words is about time. Frequency counts how many waves pass a point each second and is measured in hertz. The time period is the partner measurement: how long one single wave takes to pass the same point. On a displacement-time graph the period is read along the time axis.
keyPoints: Frequency is the number of waves passing a point each second.
Frequency carries the symbol f and is measured in hertz.
One hertz means one wave per second, so 5 Hz means five waves per second.
The time period is the time taken for a single wave to pass a point.
Period carries the symbol T and is measured in seconds.

low.restatement: Frequency counts waves arriving per second, and the time period measures how long one wave takes to arrive; they describe the same rhythm from opposite ends.
low.analogy: Buses passing a stop: frequency is buses per minute, the period is the minutes between one bus and the next.
low.examPointer: Units earn marks: frequency in hertz, period in seconds. Mixing them up is a common lost mark.

medium.restatement: On a displacement-time graph the horizontal axis is time, so the period is the horizontal repeat distance, while amplitude and wavelength stay vertical and spatial reads from other graphs.
medium.analogy: Heartbeat traces on a monitor: the spacing between beats on the time axis is the period, and the beats-per-minute rate is the frequency.
medium.examPointer: Check the horizontal axis label before reading a graph: distance gives wavelength, time gives period.

check.stem: Frequency is defined as:

options.text: the time for one wave to pass
options.explanation: That is the time period.
That is the wavelength.
That is the amplitude.

options.text: the number of waves passing a point each second
options.explanation: That count per second is what hertz measures.

check.stem: The unit of frequency is:

options.explanation: Hertz counts waves per second.
Metres measure wavelength and amplitude.
Seconds measure the time period.
Newtons measure force, not wave counts.

check.stem: A wave has frequency 5 Hz. In one second, the number of complete waves passing a point is:

options.explanation: That would be a frequency of 1 Hz.
Nothing squares the count here.
Five hertz means exactly five waves per second.
That is the period of a 5 Hz wave, not the count.

check.stem: The time period of a wave is:

options.text: the number of waves per second
options.explanation: That is the frequency.

options.text: the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point
options.explanation: That single-wave duration is the period.

options.text: the distance a wave covers in one second
options.explanation: That is the wave speed.

options.text: the time for the wave to cross the whole medium
options.explanation: The period is a single-wave measure, not a journey time.

check.stem: On a displacement-time graph, the period is read:

options.text: vertically from rest line to peak
options.explanation: That gives the amplitude.

options.text: along the time axis from the first wave to the fiftieth
options.explanation: That span covers many periods, not one.

options.text: from the graph it cannot be read
options.explanation: A time-axis graph is exactly the tool for reading periods.

options.text: along the time axis between matching points of successive waves
options.explanation: With time on the horizontal axis, the repeat spacing gives the period.

check.stem: State what is meant by the time period of a wave, with its unit.
check.modelAnswer: The time period is how long one complete cycle of the wave takes, measured in seconds.

check.stem: State what a frequency of 10 Hz means.
check.modelAnswer: Ten complete waves pass a given point every second.

check.stem: Explain why frequency and time period describe the same rhythm in opposite ways.
check.modelAnswer: Frequency counts how often a wave arrives per second while the period times one arrival, so a faster rhythm means more waves per second and a shorter time for each, making the two measures opposite views of one repetition rate.

check.stem: A displacement-time graph shows successive crests 0.02 s apart on the time axis. State the period of the wave, and what that makes the frequency.
check.modelAnswer: The period is 0.02 s, read between matching points on the time axis; a wave that repeats every 0.02 s arrives 50 times per second, so the frequency is 50 Hz.

glossary.definition: A line drawn to represent one wave, viewed from above; the spacing of the lines shows the wavelength.
The distance from the undisturbed position to a peak or a trough of a wave.
The distance from one point on a wave to the matching point on the next wave.
The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz.
The time a single wave takes to pass a point, measured in seconds.
